summary:
Bahrain repealed its British colonial-era sodomy statute in 1976 and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression as such. The 1976 penal code sets the age of adulthood for consensual same-sex acts at 21.

That baseline does not translate into safety from arrest. Police apply the morality and indecency provisions of the penal code, Articles 324, 329 and 350, which carry between three months and two years' imprisonment, fines of up to 200 Bahraini dinars, and deportation for non-Bahrainis. The government has used these articles against people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of cross-dressing. In 2009 a man was sentenced to one month in jail for wearing an abaya and carrying a purse in public; in 2011 police raided a party described as a same-sex wedding. The Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation in February 2024.

Entry is a documented vector of exposure. The Interior Minister stated that suspected effeminate homosexuals are banned from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and pending bills proposed to expressly bar LGBTQ foreigners from entry or residency. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council agreed to discuss a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners, though officials later backtracked. The indecency provisions themselves carry deportation for non-Bahrainis.

Legal gender recognition is refused at first instance. A May 2023 lower court judgment rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and declined his request for a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination. A separate 2023 court ruling held sex-reassignment procedures contrary to Islamic law where cases rest solely on gender dysphoria, limiting eligibility to people with intersex traits. Courts require medical documentation of a sex-change operation or medical necessity to change legal gender markers.

Article 330 of the penal code mandates that anyone charged with prostitution or fujoor be taken to hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and potentially relocated to a medical facility. No LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters or community organisations exist: the US Department of State reports no approved LGBTQ-related organisations, and ILGA considers registration of a sexual- or gender-diversity group improbable because the association-registration body may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order.

Bahrain has no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Hate speech against LGBTQ+ people carries no legal consequences, partly because Article 309 protects religious groups without extending equivalent protection to LGBTQ+ people. False accusations of homosexuality are used to discredit government critics, including human rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and 2011 Pearl Square demonstrators. A widely viewed 3 August 2024 Albilad caricature depicted a pride-flag roll of toilet paper captioned 'the correct place'.

Youth are an explicit policy target. A bill proposed in October 2021 would have criminalised promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to five years' imprisonment; other pending bills proposed training teachers to spot warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so children could be punished. The Education Ministry disclaims responsibility for sexuality issues: Assistant Under-Secretary Khalid Al Alawi stated it is parents' job and that the public should not make a big deal out of the problem because it does not exist, while adding that students whose appearance contradicts school values should be disciplined. On 14 February 2024 the Ministry referred a private school's administration and board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed two male students pretending to propose to each other in class; a 2022 incident in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality also prompted calls for stricter laws.

Independent human-rights researchers, including UN bodies and Amnesty International, have been denied entry or impeded for a decade, so local media often serve as the only source for this jurisdiction. The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada reported in August 2016 that, according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain; that claim contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation reading held by Wikipedia, Outright International and the 2023 US State Department, and the conflict remains unresolved.
